passage:
Mentor's note, Friday. Arohi stopped by the department office to say she had won the summer research place. She was still smiling, but by the end of the visit her voice had dropped. She told me she'd rushed to tell her partner Kamal first, and he had answered with a joke: "They must have run out of applicants." Then he changed the subject to his own exam.

She laughed it off in front of me, but her hands kept smoothing the corner of her folder. She admitted she had stopped mentioning things to him in case he sulked.

I said only that coldness at good news is worth noticing, and worth mentioning to him kindly. She said she would try, and that she had already told her hostel friends, who screamed with joy. She left looking lighter.

qa.q: What news did Arohi bring to the department office?
qa.a: She told the mentor she had won the summer research place.

qa.q: What might Arohi be feeling as she laughs off the joke while smoothing the corner of her folder?
qa.a: Hurt and unsure: her voice dropped by the end of the visit, and she had already stopped mentioning things to Kamal in case he sulked.

qa.q: What could Arohi do about Kamal's reaction to her news?
qa.a: Tell Kamal kindly how his joke landed, and keep sharing her wins with the friends who cheer for her instead of hiding them.

qa.q: What might Kamal be feeling when he answers her news with a joke and turns to his own exam?
qa.a: Kamal might feel smaller or worried about his own progress, so he may be deflecting instead of sharing her happiness.

grounding: Shows good news met with a coldness and a joke, the affected person noticing and still sharing wins with people who cheer.

passage:
Come here, Neelam, hold this onion. Your Swati Aunty has a story about a like button.

I was twenty. Aman had replied late three nights running, and then I saw him like a photo of a girl from his class. My mind ran wild: she must be his new person, that's why he's busy. I picked up his old diary at his flat and my hand stayed on it.

I put it down. Instead I made two columns on a paper: what I actually saw, and what I imagined. The left column had a late reply and a like. The right column had everything else.

Next day I said, "You've been slow to reply, and it's been worrying me. What's going on?" He'd been helping his brother move house, tired out. I felt small, and lighter.

That paper is still in my cupboard.

qa.q: What had Aman done three nights running?
qa.a: Aman had replied late three nights running.

qa.q: What was Swati thinking when she put the diary down and made two columns?
qa.a: She was trying to separate what she actually saw, a late reply and a like, from what her anxious mind was imagining.

qa.q: What made Swati's question to Aman a better choice than reading his diary?
qa.a: She asked calmly about what was worrying her, so she got the real answer, without spying or accusing him.

qa.q: How might Aman have felt if Swati had read his diary and then confronted him?
qa.a: He might have felt distrusted and invaded, and the real reason for his late replies would have been buried under the quarrel.

grounding: Shows suspicion set off by a late reply and a like, with evidence separated from anxiety and a calm question asked instead of spying.

passage:
Devika, sit with me. Your Nani, Manjula, wasn't always the person making you tea.

At twenty I was with a boy called Dinesh. One day he said I'd been flirting with a boy at the bus queue. I hadn't; he'd only asked which bus went to the market. I told him so, calmly. He grumbled, then let it go.

Two weeks later it was a classmate's notes. Then a smile at the shop. Every time I explained, and every time a new accusation came, as if my answers were never the point.

I began to wonder if I'd done something wrong. Then I stopped and looked at the pattern instead. Nothing I said ever ended it.

I told my sister everything. That's what helped me see that the problem was not my behaviour.

qa.q: Why had Dinesh said Manjula was flirting at the bus queue?
qa.a: He accused her because a boy in the queue had spoken to her, though he had only asked which bus went to the market.

qa.q: How did Manjula's thinking change when new accusations kept coming?
qa.a: She first wondered if she had done something wrong, then saw that nothing she said ever ended the accusations, so the problem was the pattern and not her behaviour.

qa.q: What helped Manjula see her situation more clearly?
qa.a: Telling her sister everything, because a trusted listener helped her see the pattern from outside.

qa.q: How might Dinesh have seen his own accusations at the time?
qa.a: He may have felt insecure and believed he was being watchful, without seeing that his suspicion had no end.

grounding: Shows being accused of things not done, answering calmly with facts, and recognising constant unfounded suspicion as a warning sign.

passage:
Charu, promise you won't laugh. Me, Rekha, the sensible one, and I've been jealous of Ishaan's exes.

He mentioned a girl from school once, just once, and I couldn't stop. I asked what they used to do on Sundays, whether he'd loved her more than me, how long they had kept texting. He answered honestly at first, and then he got tired of it. And in our last argument, I actually said, "Well, you'd have gone to her party, wouldn't you?" like a weapon.

I saw his face fall. Later, on my own, I realised the questions weren't about her at all. I was scared I'd never be as interesting as anyone before me.

So I told him that: "It's my fear, not a charge against you." He looked so relieved. We haven't talked about her since, and I don't need to.

qa.q: Which sort of questions did Rekha ask Ishaan about the girl from school?
qa.a: Rekha asked what they used to do on Sundays, whether he had loved her more than Rekha, and how long they had kept texting.

qa.q: What did Rekha realise about those questions when she thought about them alone?
qa.a: Rekha realised they were not really about the ex at all, but about a fear of never being as interesting as anyone before.

qa.q: What went wrong with the way Rekha used the past in their argument, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Rekha used the ex as a weapon and hurt Ishaan, and it improved when Rekha named the fear as Rekha's own instead of making it a charge against him.

qa.q: How does Ishaan feel during the repeated questions?
qa.a: He answers honestly at first, then gets tired, so he probably feels interrogated and worn down.

grounding: Shows jealousy about a partner's exes, with the fear named and the past no longer used as a weapon.

passage:
Warden's note, hostel B. Harish came to my room on Sunday evening looking unsettled. He explained that his partner Tara has a close friend, Ojas, who calls her late in the evenings and whom she has known since school. Harish said he felt uneasy each time the phone lit up with Ojas's name and wasn't sure whether the unease was fair.

He told me he had thought of saying, "Choose between us," and knew that would be wrong. He was rubbing the back of his neck as he spoke.

Instead, he decided to invite Ojas for chai with Tara, and to tell Tara, "I feel uneasy sometimes, and that's mine to work on. I'm not asking you to give him up." I said that sounded fair, and that I was around if he wanted to talk again.

qa.q: How long has Tara known Ojas?
qa.a: Tara has known Ojas since school.

qa.q: What does Harish's rubbing the back of his neck suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he is uncomfortable and unsure, since he says he knows an ultimatum would be wrong yet still feels uneasy when Ojas calls.

qa.q: What did Harish plan to do about his uneasiness, and why might it work?
qa.a: He planned to have chai with Ojas and Tara and to tell Tara his feeling is his to work on, which gets him to know Ojas without forcing Tara to choose.

qa.q: How might Tara see it if Harish told her to choose between him and Ojas?
qa.a: She might feel pressured and hurt, and see it as being told which friendships she is allowed to keep.

grounding: Shows uneasiness about a partner's close friend, met with getting to know them and sharing the feeling instead of an ultimatum.

passage:
Dear Preeti,

I'm writing because saying it aloud still feels impossible. Last Sunday I found messages on Nisha's phone. She had been seeing someone else for months.

For two days I couldn't eat properly. I was angry, ashamed, and then I started going back over every conversation, asking what I'd missed, what was wrong with me. I typed a message to her friends to tell them everything and deleted it.

Then your call came, and you didn't ask me to explain. Thank you.

I have decided to make no decisions for a while. I'm staying with my cousin. It was her choice, not something I caused. I can say it, though I don't quite feel it yet.

Please don't tell anyone yet. I only need you.

Jagdish

qa.q: Where is Jagdish staying for now?
qa.a: Jagdish is staying with a cousin.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling in the two days after finding the messages?
qa.a: Anger and shame, along with self-doubt, as shown by going back over every conversation to ask what was wrong.

qa.q: What did Jagdish do that was wise, and what could come next?
qa.a: Jagdish decided to make no decisions for a while and leaned on Preeti and a cousin; next Jagdish could keep talking to trusted people until feeling steadier.

qa.q: How might Preeti have felt reading Jagdish's letter?
qa.a: Preeti probably felt honoured to be trusted and worried for Jagdish, and would want to respect the request for privacy.

grounding: Shows the shock, shame and self-doubt of discovering a partner's cheating, with time, friends and the reminder that it was their choice.

passage:
The metro was almost empty at midnight, and Aparna was still smiling at the window. Tarun had walked her to the station after the department party, and at the platform he had kissed her. She'd let him. Her heart was racing with something bright and forbidden.

By the second station, the brightness had turned into a cold weight. Her phone buzzed: Akash, asking if she'd reached safely, telling her to sleep well. She read it three times.

She had told herself lately that Akash was too busy to notice her. That was true. It also wasn't a reason. She'd chosen this.

At home she blocked Tarun's number, then sat on the edge of her bed. Tomorrow she would ask Akash to meet, tell him plainly, and not blame him. Her stomach ached at the thought.

qa.q: Where did Tarun kiss Aparna?
qa.a: He kissed her at the platform after the department party.

qa.q: What was Aparna feeling by the second station, and how does the passage show it?
qa.a: She felt dread and guilt, since the brightness turned into a cold weight, and she read Akash's message three times.

qa.q: What did Aparna do that ends the deception, and what will she face next?
qa.a: She blocked Tarun's number and planned to tell Akash plainly without blaming him; next she has to face how he reacts and accept the consequences.

qa.q: How might Akash feel if he hears about the kiss from Aparna herself instead of finding out elsewhere?
qa.a: He would probably be hurt and angry, but he may also see that she chose to be honest rather than hiding it.

grounding: Shows crossing a line with a thrill then guilt and dread, and a first step toward honest admission without blaming the partner.

passage:
Monday. Zaid told Farida everything in the college garden, before she had asked. She sat with her arms wrapped around her knees and said, "I can't say I forgive you. I don't know what I feel." He nodded and left her alone.

Saturday. On the hostel roof, Farida's friend Nandini passed her a cup of tea. "If you say yes now, is it because you want to, or because you're scared of being alone?" Farida looked at the water tank for a long time. "Scared," she said. "Mostly." Nandini didn't say anything. She just stayed.

Three weeks later. Zaid had answered every question honestly, even the ones that shamed him, and hadn't asked her to hurry. Farida told him, "I'm not there yet. Maybe I won't be. I'm not deciding to punish you. I'm just deciding slowly."

That night she slept the whole night.

qa.q: Where did Zaid tell Farida everything?
qa.a: He told her in the college garden.

qa.q: What does Farida admit to Nandini about why she might say yes?
qa.a: She admits she is mostly scared of being alone, which shows she does not want to forgive just to escape loneliness.

qa.q: What made it easier for Farida to take her time over three weeks?
qa.a: Zaid answered every question honestly, even the shaming ones, and did not ask her to hurry, while Nandini stayed with her without pushing.

qa.q: How might Zaid feel when Farida says she may never be there?
qa.a: He may feel worried and regretful, but he can see she is not punishing him, only giving herself honest time.

grounding: Shows wondering whether trust is possible after betrayal, with forgiveness left slow and unforced, and walking away kept as an option.

passage:
"Didi, I have to tell Rahul. I can't breathe."

"Tell him what, exactly?" Payal put down the dal spoon.

"About last month. About Kabir. It was one evening. It won't happen again."

"Okay. Why now?"

"Because I can't stand this. Every time he smiles at me I feel sick. If I tell him, I'll feel lighter."

"Lighter." Payal sat across from her. "And Rahul?"

Indu stared at the table. "He'll be hurt."

"Yes. He'll be carrying it, and you'll feel better. Is that the reason?"

"I don't know." Indu pressed her palms to her eyes. "Maybe part of it. Maybe I also don't want him to keep trusting a lie."

"Then tell him that. And be ready for him to be angry, and to want space, and not to comfort you. Are you?"

"...No. But I'll do it anyway."

qa.q: Who is Indu going to tell?
qa.a: Indu wants to tell Rahul.

qa.q: What is Indu feeling when she says every smile from Rahul makes her feel sick?
qa.a: Deep guilt, and a wish to be relieved of it; she says she can't breathe and is sure she will feel lighter after telling him.

qa.q: What does Payal ask Indu to be ready for before telling Rahul?
qa.a: To be ready for Rahul to be angry, want space and not comfort her, so the confession is not about getting relief from him.

qa.q: How might Rahul feel if Indu confessed and then expected him to comfort her?
qa.a: He might feel his hurt was being pushed aside and that he had been handed her guilt to carry.

grounding: Shows guilt after cheating with a wish to confess for relief, weighed against what confession serves and its fallout.
